title: Supervised learning & the standard workflow
intro: Before we look at logistic regression and SVMs, we lay the foundation: what supervised learning actually is and which fixed steps you always follow in scikit-learn. Everything that follows — loss functions, regularisation, kernels — builds on this pattern.

blocks.html:
In supervised learning you learn a mapping between inputs and outputs, based on examples. By convention the inputs are called X (features) and the outputs y (targets). In the newsgroups dataset from the course, the features are derived from the words occurring in each article (about 130,000 features) and y is the topic of the article — exactly the thing we want to predict. With ~11,000 training examples you learn a function that classifies new articles.

There are two flavours: classification (the y values are categories, such as "good/not-good" or "spam/not spam") and regression (the y values are continuous numbers, such as a price or a temperature). This course is about classification — and within classification, about the two most popular linear classifiers: logistic regression and support vector machines.
Supervised learning = learning from examples of input-output pairs (X, y), so that you can predict the correct output for new input.

sections.title: The scikit-learn workflow: fit → predict → score

blocks.html: The beauty of scikit-learn is that every model has the same syntax, whether you use KNN, logistic regression or an SVM. There are four fixed steps: import the class, instantiate (this is where you set hyperparameters, such as the number of neighbours for KNN), fit with fit(X, y), and afterwards predict with predict or evaluate with score. A hyperparameter is a choice you make before fitting and it controls the complexity of the model.

blocks.caption: The complete workflow with KNN on the digits dataset
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# 1. Load the data: X = images (8x8 pixels), y = digit 0-9
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
print('X shape:', X.shape, '| y shape:', y.shape)

# 2. Instantiate + set hyperparameters
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)

# 3. Fit on the training data
knn.fit(X, y)

# 4. Predict and score
y_pred = knn.predict(X)
print('First 5 predictions:', y_pred[:5])
print('True digits        :', y[:5])
print('Training score     :', round(knn.score(X, y), 3))

blocks.html: y_pred contains one prediction per row of X — even when you call predict on the training data itself, as above.

sections.title: Generalising: why a test score is mandatory

blocks.html:
The training score above is almost 100% — but that says little. What we really want to know is whether the model generalises to data it has never seen. The standard solution is a validation/test set: with train_test_split you keep 25% of the examples apart by default. Important: you refit the model on the training set only, because once the model has seen the test set during fitting, the test set has lost its purpose.

In the course, KNN's score on the newsgroups data drops from ~100% (train) to ~66% (test). Whether that is "good" depends on the situation — but the training error was in any case a poor prediction of how the model classifies new data.

blocks.label: accuracy
blocks.caption: The score function of scikit-learn classifiers computes accuracy by default.
Honest evaluation with train_test_split
blocks.source:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# Fit ONLY on the training set
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)
knn.fit(X_train, y_train)

print('Train score:', round(knn.score(X_train, y_train), 3))
print('Test score :', round(knn.score(X_test,  y_test), 3))

blocks.html: Never train on the test set. The test set is a "simulation" of new data — as soon as the model sees it during fitting, you are no longer measuring generalisation but memorisation.
